 Leaked documents reveal Deutsche Bank's role in Israeli submarine deals
 Leaked documents show Deutsche Bank approved 11,600 arms deals worth over $200 billion despite human rights warnings, financing major German defense firms and weapons sales involving Israel, including submarines, while also backing deals with Qatar 
 Zeev Avrahami, Berlin | Add a comment Print Find an error? Report us Related Topics Banks document leak Germany The arms industry is booming amid wars around the world , and Deutsche Bank wants a piece of the pie. Wednesday's massive leak of 15 million bank documents reveals how the German financial giant financed deals despite internal warnings and sheds light on its role in arms transactions involving Israel. According to the documents, even concerns that ThyssenKrupp (TKMS) submarines could carry nuclear weapons did not deter the bank. The disclosure of internal documents leaked by two bank employees continues to reverberate, driving down Deutsche Bank's share price and further tarnishing its already battered reputation. Initial revelations showed how the bank turned a blind eye to warnings from regulators and continued providing banking services to Russian oligarchs , Jeffrey Epstein and Donald Trump. Now, it has emerged that the bank spent decades financing arms deals worth hundreds of billions of euros. Gallery Deutsche Bank ( Photo: Mark Lennihan/AP ) Germany's largest bank also ignored internal risk assessments in its arms dealings, becoming a financial partner to the country's leading defense manufacturers. The wars in Ukraine and Iran and Israel's multifront war have turned the arms industry into a thriving, lucrative business. Deutsche Bank became a major financier and lender to Rheinmetall, Diehl Defence, Renk, Airbus and other companies in Germany's defense industry. According to the leaked documents, nearly 13,000 requests for arms transactions were submitted to the bank's oversight committees between 2000 and 2015. Most came with clear warnings that the weapons could be used in serious human rights violations in war zones. The bank approved 11,600 of those requests, involving transactions worth more than $200 billion. The limits: Chemical weapons, land mines and cluster bombs 
 Israel is featured prominently in the leaked documents, which identify Israeli defense companies Rafael and Elbit among Deutsche Bank's business partners. Financing arms deals involving Israel presents a reputational dilemma for Deutsche Bank. While its risk assessment division advises against involvement in arms transactions because of the potential damage to the bank's public image, Deutsche Bank also wants to avoid being seen as unwilling to support Israel and efforts to strengthen the IDF. At the same time, Deutsche Bank is far less selective when it comes to economic opportunities. It also provides financial assistance and brokerage services for arms sales to countries hostile to Israel, such as Qatar. Merkava tank. Mentioned in the leaked documents ( Photo: Jalaa MAREY / AFP ) According to the documents, the bank does draw certain lines: It does not allow any of its divisions to finance transactions involving cluster munitions, land mines or chemical, biological and nuclear weapons. Beyond those restrictions, however, almost anything goes. If a deal offers an opportunity for profit and is not explicitly prohibited, the bank approves it. In 2023, Germany exported 326.5 million euros worth of weapons to Israel. That figure was cut in half the following year after Germany imposed restrictions on arms exports to Israel. Deutsche Bank was a major player in financing those exports. But the documents show that the bank was also involved in providing guarantees and loans before the war. Between January 2021 and August 2023, Deutsche Bank supported companies including Boeing, Leonardo and Rolls-Royce in arms transactions involving Israel. The bank provided approximately 4 billion euros in guarantees and loans for those deals. The submarine deal: When the rules bend 
 Deutsche Bank was willing to finance deals of virtually any size. It backed a relatively small 38 million-euro transaction involving Renk's sale of approximately 80 gearboxes for Israel's Merkava tanks. But it also participated in the sale of submarines to Israel by the naval division of German industrial conglomerate TKMS, in a deal worth more than 3 billion euros. INS Drakon ( Photo: IDF Spokesperson's Unit ) The submarine deal also demonstrated how Deutsche Bank's rules could be bent to accommodate business interests. The bank had declared certain restrictions on weapons financing, as noted above, and pledged not to participate in transactions suspected of involving corruption, financial crimes or money laundering. But TKMS was an extremely important client, and the submarine deal with Israel was crucial to the conglomerate. This time, Deutsche Bank turned a blind eye to the possibility that the submarines could be armed with nuclear weapons. Who leaked the documents? 
 Wednesday's massive leak, which has shaken Deutsche Bank, exposed misconduct, systemic failures, unprofessional behavior, unfulfilled promises of reform and secrets involving some of the bank's billionaire and oligarch clients, including U.S. President Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein. The leaked material includes emails, internal investigations, minutes of board meetings, compliance files — records maintained by the department responsible for ensuring that the bank follows laws and regulations — and employee chat conversations. The documents shed new light on the career of CEO Christian Sewing, who took over in 2018. Sewing is generally credited with rescuing the scandal-plagued bank from the brink of collapse and steering it toward record profits. According to the documents, however, the man who promised to put an end to the bank's string of scandals was privately pushing for greater risk-taking, railing against the compliance department and concealing some of the bank's problems from shareholders. The investigation, titled Inside Deutsche Bank, also exposes accounting tricks and financial reporting that bordered on deception. It provides previously unknown details about the bank's relationships with Trump and Epstein. Christian Sewing, Jeffrey Epstein and Donald Trump ( Photo: Kirill Kudryavtsev, Michael Probst, Aaron Schwartz, New York State Sex Offender Registry, AFP, AP, REUTERS ) The two whistleblowers were motivated primarily by Deutsche Bank's ties to Russian oligarchs and Russian money. They copied the documents and handed them over to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife. In a statement, the whistleblowers said they acted in the "public interest" to expose the bank's conduct, including "issues such as accounts held by Russian oligarchs." One added that "the bank needs a complete overhaul in management and culture." One of them added that "the bank needs a complete overhaul of its management and culture." In response, Deutsche Bank said the issues raised "date back many years, in some cases decades" and had, where relevant, been discussed with regulators. "We are a different bank today. Under Christian Sewing's leadership, Deutsche Bank has gone through a fundamental transformation," the bank said. Deutsche Bank added that it invested 7 billion euros in strengthening its internal controls between 2019 and 2025, and that its progress "has been recognised by the market, key regulators and supervisory authorities, as well as clients and other stakeholders."
